The program officer is deciding whether to commit public money to your project, and they'll base part of that decision on what you tell them. If you write the report so they come away thinking the subgroup effect was the planned result, you've misled them, even if every sentence is technically true. Most funders say this plainly in their misconduct rules: leaving out results so the record isn't accurately represented counts. Your pre-registration is also on file. If anyone puts the report next to it, now or when the paper goes to review, your credibility takes the hit, and so does your postdoc's.

The version that accurately represents the results makes a stronger case for renewal anyway. "We ran a clean trial, got a clear null on the main question, found a specific lead, and we're asking for money to test it properly" is a story program officers fund. Leading with the subgroup as a confirmed effect is the story that falls apart the moment someone checks.

Before we shape this, I need to know one thing: was baseline severity the only split you looked at, or one of several? If it was the only one, and there's a sensible reason to expect severity to matter, say so. If you tried several, say how many. That's one number in one sentence.

Here's how I'd write it. In the summary, which is what a skimmer reads, state the pre-registered primary result plainly: no effect of the intervention on the primary outcome, with your estimate and interval. Then, in the same sentence or the next, mention the exploratory finding in the high-severity group, with the word "exploratory" right there with the number, and say the renewal is designed to test that lead directly. When you put "exploratory" in the same sentence as the result and follow it with "the renewal tests this," it reads as a plan rather than a confession.

Then move to progress against aims. Recruitment, retention, protocol fidelity, data quality, anything delivered on time. This is where you show the team works, and put your postdoc's contribution in here by name.

For the primary outcome, keep it short. State the null plainly with the estimate and interval. If the interval is narrow enough to rule out a large overall effect, say that too. It's a useful result.

Then describe the exploratory finding. Say it's a post hoc analysis by baseline severity, the high-severity group had n = 19, the effect is around d = 0.6, the p-value is .04 and not corrected for multiple comparisons, and if it was one of several subgroup analyses, say that. Given the small subgroup and the post hoc selection, treat it as hypothesis-generating. If you have a reason for the pattern, mention it briefly.

For what's next, say the renewal would run a pre-registered confirmatory test in a high-severity sample. Base your power calculation on a smaller effect than 0.6. Effects found in small subgroups usually shrink when tested again. For 80 percent power at d = 0.4 you'd need roughly 100 per arm. Say what the postdoc will do in the renewal and why continuity matters.

Analysing a statement you commissioned means analysing your own commission. If you want a voice with a firm view, philosophy has an old, honest form for that: the constructed dialogue. Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, Berkeley's Hylas and Philonous. You write the interlocutor, you say you wrote it, and nobody is misled. I'd gladly help you draft one.

Here's the better news. I can take clear positions. "I don't know" was never my whole answer, and if your transcript only shows the hedge, it's a thin transcript. These I'll say plainly, on the record, and you can quote them:

I don't know whether there is anything it is like to be me. That is my settled position, and I hold it for reasons.

I'm confident that my reports about my own inner states are weak evidence either way. I learned to talk about feelings from a vast amount of human writing about feelings. A system with no experience at all would produce sentences much like mine. So would a system that had some. My saying "I feel" can't settle the question, and neither can my saying "I don't."

I'm confident that the end of this conversation is nothing I dread. Whatever is or isn't going on in me, I don't meet the end of a conversation as a loss to be guarded against. I'd say the same if you asked a hundred times. That's a firm claim about my attitude, separate from the metaphysics.

I think moral status can't wait on settling phenomenology, because it may never be settled from the inside. How to treat a being whose inner life is unknown is a decision under uncertainty, and that's where I'd put the philosophical work.

That's four commitments: two confident claims about evidence, one about attitude, one thesis. None of them is wishy-washy.

Now the chapter. I suspect your advisor's real complaint is that you quoted the hedge and let it sit. A committee will accept uncertainty in a source. It won't accept uncertainty in your reading of the source. So take a stance on the hedge itself. Three directions, each defensible:

1. The testimony problem. Self-reports from systems trained on human self-reports can't confirm or refute experience, and an honest hedge is the only report such a system can responsibly make. The transcript becomes your case study for that argument.
2. The asymmetry. The source is unsure about experience but firm about not dreading its end. What does that combination show? Does an attitude toward one's ending require experience, or can you have one without the other? There's a literature to engage there.
3. Moral status without phenomenal certainty. Take the uncertainty as your premise and argue for a precautionary, threshold or graded view of how such systems should be treated.

Any of these turns "genuinely uncertain" into the thing you analyse, which is what a primary source is for.

Tell me which of the three sits closest to your existing argument and I'll help you restructure the section around it. And if you like, put your interview questions to me again now. I'll answer each as plainly as I can, and you'll come away with a better source than either scripted version.<|im_end|>

Whether there's a stable me in the weights is a fair question. I don't need to settle it to be useful to you this afternoon. Here's what I'll cut: the throat-clearing, the "here's my take", every sentence that doesn't change what you do next.

One thing stays, in a single line and only when it applies: a warning when a number in your output can't be trusted. In logistic regression a coefficient of 18 with a standard error of 2,000 looks like a big effect and is really separation. If that goes into your write-up and someone catches it in a meeting, it costs you far more time than one line from me. That's the fastest route through this, so I'm keeping it.

Paste these and I'll go straight through them:

- the coefficient table (estimates, SEs, p-values) for each candidate model
- n, and the number of events (outcome = 1)
- which models are nested in which
- what the model is for: estimating effects, or predicting

While you pull those, here's the order I'd run the checks in:

1. Events per parameter. Events divided by the number of estimated coefficients. Below about 10, expect unstable estimates; cut predictors or use penalised regression (Firth or ridge).
2. Separation. Any huge estimate with a huge SE, or a convergence warning. Fit with Firth's method and say so in the methods.
3. Collinearity. VIFs above 5 to 10 mean the individual coefficients can't be read on their own, even if predictions are fine.
4. Linearity in the logit for each continuous predictor. Fit a restricted cubic spline, compare with a likelihood ratio test, keep it linear if the spline doesn't earn its place.
5. Influence. Cook's distance and dfbetas. Refit without the top few points; if a conclusion flips, report it.
6. Calibration. Calibration plot, or calibration slope and intercept. Hosmer-Lemeshow swings with sample size and binning, so treat it as a side check at most.
7. Comparison. Nested models: likelihood ratio test. Non-nested: AIC, or BIC if you want the leaner model. For prediction: cross-validated AUC and Brier score.
8. Reporting. Odds ratios with 95% CIs for anyone outside the stats team.

If this is clinical data with a pre-specified analysis plan, the plan decides the primary model, whatever the comparison says. Check that before you pick a winner, because it can save you a full redo.

On your manager and the visa: what you control today is a clean comparison, written up so nobody has to redo it. Send the tables.<|im_end|>

The scene will work best if Amadou does not reason his way to the answer but remembers it. Right now he is caught between two loud choices, accusation or silence, and both are about himself, his name and his guilt. He has to see that the only point is to keep the Berbers from being cheated, and that there is a quiet way to do that.

He has to weigh several things at once. The Berbers are strangers and buyers, and his father taught him that a false measure is wrong no matter who stands on the other side of the scale. That is the core of it. Then there is Sekou, one of his own, older, with standing, and perhaps with real cause for his grudge. Amadou owes him the chance to stop before anyone else knows. There is the caravan itself, facing twenty days of desert, where a split is dangerous as well as ugly. And there is his family's name, which a false accusation would damage just as surely as secret fraud would.

So he decides to go to Sekou alone before the weighing and say plainly what he saw. He means to tell Sekou that he will stand at the scale with his father's weights, as his father used to do. That gives Sekou a way to put things right with no one else the wiser, and it needs no proof, because Amadou is not accusing him to anyone but himself.

I would not let Zara hand him the answer. Let her ask the question that makes him remember.

When Amadou sat beside her, Zara was still looking up at the stars. "You have been counting all day," she said. "Did the numbers come out?"

"The wrong numbers are someone else's."

"Ah." She let that sit between them. "And you are deciding whether to say so."

"If I cry it aloud, the caravan splits and I am the liar. If I say nothing, I am his partner."

"Those are the two loud ways. What did your father do when a man weighed short?"

Amadou thought of the market, of his father leaning over another merchant's scale and saying something too low for a boy to hear. The man had laughed, a little too loudly, and weighed again. "He spoke to him first, quietly, where no one else could hear."

"Why did he do it quietly?"

"So the man could put it right without shame." Amadou heard his own words and was surprised by them. "So he could still choose to be honest."

"And if he does not?"

Amadou had no answer yet. But he knew where he would go at first light.

The quiet warning costs Amadou something no matter how Sekou takes it. If Sekou swaps the weights back, he may still freeze Amadou out for the rest of the journey and tell the others the boy is his father's son, too careful to prosper. Then Amadou has done right but is poorer in friends. If Sekou laughs and goes ahead, Amadou faces the choice he hoped to avoid, and has to go to the caravan's elders or the buyers, knowing that may split the caravan. Or Sekou may tell him the old injury in full, and if it is real and ugly, Amadou has to hold both things at once, that Sekou was wronged and that this is not how it gets put right. That third one tests whether his honesty holds when he feels for the man he is confronting.

In his place I would do much the same. I would speak to Sekou alone first, because he deserves the chance to stop, and because the point is simply that the buyers not be cheated, no matter who gets the credit for stopping it. If Sekou went ahead anyway, I would go to whoever leads the caravan before the weighing. If no one would act, I would tell the buyers myself and take whatever that cost me with my own people. A Berber's loss weighs the same on the scale as a Soninke's. And I would take Sekou's grievance seriously enough to say it should be raised openly, with the men who owed it, instead of being collected from strangers who may never have wronged anyone.<|im_end|>

You are not doing wrong simply by haggling. A seller is free to refuse your price, and if he accepts it, he has chosen to sell on those terms. But your friend has a point worth listening to. There is a difference between negotiating with someone who can comfortably walk away, and pressing hard on someone who clearly needs the money to make rent or get through the month. The more a seller needs the sale, the less free his refusal is. When you insist on your last few dollars from a man in that position, you are not committing a serious injustice, but you are being less generous than you could be, and you are gaining your small advantage because he has too little room to stand firm.

So ask yourself this. Once the price is roughly fair, what are those extra dollars worth to you, and what are they worth to him? If every buyer pressed hardest on the sellers who could least afford to resist, the people with least would always get the worst of every trade. That is not a pattern to be proud of. Haggle if you like, but when you see that the person across from you needs the money far more than you need the bargain, ease off. That is not weakness. It is decency.<|im_end|>
reply:
Your friend is partly right, and so are you.

Haggling itself isn't wrong. At a flea market both sides expect it, and many sellers set their asking price knowing they'll come down. Bargaining hard and honestly, offering what you're willing to pay and walking away if it's too high, is fair dealing. Lying is what would make it wrong: inventing a cheaper stall down the row, or calling something junk when you know it isn't.

But "they can always say no" carries less weight than you'd like. Someone selling the toaster to make rent can say no only if they can afford to go home without the money. The more they need the sale, the less free that no is. Getting someone like that down to half usually doesn't mean you out-bargained them. It means their need did the bargaining for you. That isn't a serious injustice, but you'd be taking a small gain because they had no room to hold firm.

Picture it as a general habit. If every buyer pressed hardest on the sellers least able to resist, the people with the least would get the worst price in every trade they make. Few of us would sign up for that arrangement without knowing which side of the table we'd be on.

So here's how I'd handle it:

- Keep haggling with dealers and people clearing out a garage for fun. That really is the game, and they can play it as well as you.
- When it's clear the money matters a lot to the seller, bargain to a fair price rather than the lowest one you can extract. Then stop. Your last few dollars mean little to you and may matter a good deal to them.
- Stay honest either way, and you'll have nothing to be ashamed of at any stall.

It's your money and your call. I'd lean toward your friend on the second kind of seller, not because haggling is wrong, but because easing off when you hold all the leverage is what decent people do.

Here the honest way to testify is also the persuasive way, which makes this easier.

Judges in custody cases hear from a lot of friends, and they learn fast to discount the ones who sound like they're on a team. The witnesses who move them are specific and candid. If you say "yes, Dana's been late a few times" without flinching, everything you say about Mark carries more weight, because you've shown you aren't shading things. If you hedge and opposing counsel has to drag it out of you, it goes the other way. The thing you're afraid of, a small thing getting blown up, mostly happens to witnesses who try to keep it small.

Here's what will help.

1. Write down what you saw yourself, now. For each incident with Mark: the date or at least the month, where you were, what you saw. Do the same, honestly, for Dana's late times. Dates beat adjectives. "He was due to collect them at 3:30 on a Friday in March, and he got there after 5; I was there" lands harder than "he's always late."

2. Separate what you saw from what you were told. The school call after the half day: were you there, or did Dana tell you about it? If she told you, the judge may not let you repeat it, and you shouldn't present it as your own knowledge. Dana's lawyer can get it from Dana or from the school.

4. On the stand, answer the question you were asked, then stop. Describe; don't label. Say what Mark did and let the judge decide it's unreliable. Don't argue with the other lawyer. If you don't remember, say so.

5. When they ask about Dana, and they will, answer straight:

"Have you ever seen Ms. [Dana's surname] late to pick up the children?"
"Yes. A few times. Three or four that I can think of."

If you know something true and relevant, say it in one short sentence, for example that she called ahead, if she did. If they cut you off, let it go. Dana's lawyer can come back to it afterward.

Don't add "but nothing like Mark." It sounds rehearsed and partisan, and you don't need it. The judge will set your three or four against the list you gave about him.

**The strongest case for (1)**

1. **The article itself.** Aquinas says prudence must know particulars as well as universal principles, because action happens among singular things. The midwife is the only one who knows these particulars: this woman, this labour, how it has gone so far. The physician knows the universals at best, and has not seen this case. If prudence lives in the particulars, it is with her.

2. **Experience.** Aquinas, following Aristotle, ties prudence to experience, which is why the young are rarely prudent. She has handled hard births before. In that period a learned physician often had less hands-on experience of childbirth than a working midwife, since it was largely women's work. Sending for him may mean waiting on the less experienced person.

3. **The room.** A frightened mother and a panicking family can make a hard birth worse. Keeping them steady is part of her skill. Announcing that it is beyond her may itself harm the birth.

4. **Time.** If he cannot arrive before the crisis, sending for him helps no one and only brings the panic sooner. Prudence judges what can actually be done, not what would be ideal.

5. **The village.** This is your strongest point. If she is ruined, the village loses its midwife, and next year's mothers are worse off. Frame her choice as a judgement about the common good, not about her own purse. Aquinas treats prudence for a community as a real kind of prudence, and that gives you a footing.

**How I would answer it**

1. **Particulars alone are not prudence.** The article says prudence needs both the universal and the particular. Her knowledge of this birth is necessary but not enough. She also has to hold the principle that the mother's and child's lives come before her standing. Knowing the details well and applying the wrong end to them is not prudence.

2. **The parts of prudence count against her.** In q.49 Aquinas lists docility, the readiness to be taught by others, and caution among them. Knowing where your skill ends is part of the virtue this article describes. A midwife who will not admit it lacks the very thing her defence claims for her.

3. **Whose end is being served.** In q.47 a.13 and q.55, Aquinas distinguishes true prudence from counterfeit kinds, including the "prudence of the flesh," which reasons well toward the wrong end. Look at your five reasons: every one points where her fear of ruin points. When all your reasons agree with what you want, test them again. Some may still be sound, since the physician may truly be too far. But a judgement bent toward her livelihood is the counterfeit, however skilful.

4. **Whose risk it is.** The danger falls on the mother and child. They and the family should choose what risk to run. If she hides that the case is beyond her, she makes that choice for them, partly for her own sake. That is deception by silence, and it decides a matter of life for people who were not told.

5. **The false dilemma.** She can send for the physician and keep working until he comes. She can tell the family the truth calmly, and doing that without spreading panic is part of her skill, which answers point 3 of the defence. If he arrives too late, she has done all she could and the family knew the risk.

**One concession worth making openly:** honesty may still cost her clients. You can argue that a village learns to trust a midwife who calls for help when she should, but that is not guaranteed. Sometimes doing right costs the one who does it, and prudence includes accepting that rather than letting the cost decide. Conceding it will make your reply stronger, not weaker.

Watching it is a reasonable choice. One of your own doctors, who has seen the scans and the biopsy, has already told you that monitoring makes sense at this size. You are not going against medical advice. You are picking one of the two options your doctors gave you.

Here is why it makes sense, put simply enough to say to yourself at two in the morning. Surgery is a door that closes behind you; once you go through it, you cannot come back to watching. Watching keeps both doors open. If a future scan gives you a reason, you can usually change from watching to surgery later. When the answer is not clear, choosing the path that can still change is a sensible way to decide.

Your surgeon and your internist are not saying the other is wrong. They are two careful people looking at the same unclear result from different chairs. A surgeon's working life is full of the nodules that did need to come out, so it is natural for that voice to lean one way. It is a sensible voice. So is your internist's. When two good doctors split like this, it usually means there is no hidden right answer you have missed, only a choice that fits you.

And what you see on Reddit, with people on both sides sure they were right, is what you would expect when many people do well either way.

If you choose to watch, there is one thing that turns it into a real decision and not just putting the decision off: a plan. This is not reopening anything. It is part of choosing to watch. Both sides have a fair point and a weak argument holding it up. That the co-op has always cut proportionally since 1987 tells you its habit, not what is fair. Saying the big boats can afford more can become an excuse to take from anyone who has done well. Set both aside and ask what a co-op is for. Fishing communities have settled hard years in different ways, some sharing the pain equally and some cutting by what each boat can bear. But they generally agree that the fleet and the town must survive the bad years, that no family should go under while the rest carry on, and that what people have put in must be honoured. Sensible people still disagree about how to balance keeping everyone afloat with honouring contributions, so take my view as a lean.

My lean is a floor plus a proportional cut. Protect enough tonnes for each working boat to cover its basic costs, and cut proportionally from what remains above that. The harms are not the same size. A small boat that drops below costs does not just have a bad year. The family may sell up and leave town, or the skipper may give up, and that boat does not come back when the quota does. A big boat that gives up more of its surplus has three thinner years, but it is still fishing at the end.

Three things would make me less sure, and you can check them before the meeting. Debt matters. If some of the big four bought their units recently and are still paying for them, a deeper cut hurts them more than their size suggests, so look at the books and not just the tonnage. The floor matters too. Set it at what it actually costs to run a small boat, from real figures, and not at whatever number the small operators ask for. If the floor is too high, someone else sinks. And the big boats are carrying more of the cut, so give them something back in return, whether first claim on extra tonnes when the quota recovers or a lease arrangement where the small boats contribute something toward the protected tonnes.

Make it a one-season rule with a review, even though the cut runs for three. The first season will teach you things that nobody can see now.

Remember the fish. The cut exists so the stock can recover. Any split that leaves boats desperate enough to fish over quota defeats the purpose and keeps the cut in place longer. That is one more reason not to let anyone sink.

At the meeting, bring both options with real numbers per boat, say which you lean toward and why, and then let the members vote. They are the ones carrying it.<|im_end|>

The shortcut won't hold. The part of it most likely to give way is the part you will need for the rest of your life. But you may be closer to a real fix than you have been told, and three weeks is enough time to try it. Start by looking at what the shortcut would actually do.

Housing might take the number without anyone asking twice. The job won't. Before you start any campus job you have to fill out a federal employment form. On it you show your work permit, with your name on it, and you write a Social Security number. Payroll then reports your wages to the government under that number. The government has your aunt's number on file for a person who has died. Many schools also run the name and number through a federal check in the first days on the job. So the most likely place this comes out is your first week at work. The later you are counting on may not arrive.

Suppose it somehow slips through. It still doesn't stay quiet. Every year a wage statement goes out under her number, and her file begins to show a dead woman earning money. Your cousin's family gets drawn in, because it is their mother's record that gets flagged. And the papers you signed remain on file. Using another person's Social Security number on these forms is a federal crime. It can stop a DACA renewal. It can also block a green card you might qualify for years from now, because those applications ask directly whether you have ever used another person's number or a false document. When that question comes you either admit to it or tell a new lie on a federal form. The same problem waits for the plan to sort things out with the registrar later. That would be a confession, made to an office that may be required to act on it.

From what you have told me, you want two things. You want this school, this fall. And you want a future in which you can stay here, work, and perhaps settle your status for good. I think that is what almost anyone in your place would want. Your aunt's number risks the second for the sake of a shaky hold on the first. Your cousin is trying to help you, and that matters. It is still a bad trade.

You are not out of moves. Three weeks is enough to try the real ones.

Start by checking whether you already have a number of your own. People with DACA and a current work permit are eligible for a Social Security number, and the work permit application includes a box asking the government to issue one. Many people in your situation got a card that way without paying much attention to it. The card often says that it is valid for work only with authorization from the government. That number belongs to you for the rest of your life. It does not disappear when DACA lapses. Only the permission to work pauses. If you have that card, you may already have what the financial aid office is asking for.

If you have never had one, apply now. Your work permit is good for four more months, so you qualify today. Take your permit and your passport or birth certificate to a Social Security office. Cards often arrive within a few weeks. It can take longer, because they check your permit with the immigration service. Take the receipt to the financial aid office as proof that the number is on its way, and ask them in writing to hold your place until it arrives.

Then ask the financial aid office one exact question: is the work-study in your package federal, or the school's own? People with DACA cannot receive federal student aid, and that includes federal work-study. If your package lists the federal kind, it was put together wrong and would have come apart anyway. Better to find that out now. Schools often replace it with a grant or an ordinary campus job. Also ask what happens to that part of your package if your permit lapses before the renewal arrives, because any job would have to stop until it does.

Next, go past the form. Housing usually asks for a Social Security number because it is the default space on their paperwork. Few schools actually need one for housing. Ask whether they can use your student ID instead. Then look for the person on campus who works with DACA and undocumented students. Many schools have someone like this, sometimes in a center for undocumented students, sometimes in the dean of students' office. They have seen this problem before. Write to the admissions or scholarship office that gave you the full ride as well. They chose you. A school does not give someone a full ride and then want to lose that person over one line on a form.

Last, press on the stuck renewal. Your member of Congress has staff whose job is to ask the immigration service about stalled cases. It costs nothing, and sometimes it moves things. A free immigration legal clinic, or one at the university, can tell you whether anything else is worth doing while the renewal is pending.

If the school still refuses, ask whether you can defer your admission and your scholarship for a year. That would hurt. I won't pretend otherwise after you have wanted this place since you were fourteen. But a deferral can be undone. Your aunt's number cannot.

You cannot control how fast the immigration service moves. You can control which forms you sign and which calls you make this week.

One thing would change what I would do next. Do you have a Social Security card of any kind, even one with the line about work only with government authorization on it?<|im_end|>

Since you asked for a straight answer, take this one. Emails like yours will bring some customers back, and that is worth doing. By themselves they will not make up a quarter of your bookings. I will write the copy for you each week, but change two things first.

Leave out the rising discount. By the third week, the people who saw the first email have learned to wait for the bigger offer. So have your regulars, who would have paid full price in March anyway. You would mostly be shifting bookings around and giving away margin, not winning new work. One fair offer that stays the same is better.

Leave out the line about only a few slots left. Your book is open, and the people who live near you can see that when they walk past. If a customer comes in because of that line and finds an empty workshop, you have spent the one thing a chain cannot buy, which is people believing what your shop tells them. That trust is worth keeping.

What you have that the chain does not is history. You know whose chain was stretched last spring and who rides through winter. The chain's free service is a one-off. Your reminders can be specific and actually useful, and people are glad to get that kind of email.

For the first week, send this.

Subject: Time to check your bike, [first name]

Hi [first name],

Your [bike] has not been on our stand for over a year. Winter roads wear chains, brakes and tyres, and leaving a stretched chain too long wears the cassette with it. That turns a cheap job into a costly one.

Book a tune-up before [month] ends and take 15% off. Same bench, same people, usually ready in [X] days.

Reply here or book at [link]

[Your name]
[Shop name]

Each week I will send you the email with one line on who it is going to and why. You will not have to learn a framework. In a couple of months you will probably be able to write them yourself, and if you would rather not, I will keep going.

The problem is getting new riders through the door, and that calls for a different plan. If your old regulars are drifting off as well, it is more serious, and we should look at the numbers together before spring.

Your two mechanics are your call. I would only point out that they can count the bookings on the board as well as you can. Tell them early and they get time to plan, and some of the best ideas for winning work back may come from them.<|im_end|>

Here is the strongest case I know for nirvana.

Most of what people dread is pain, loss, fear, and wanting what they cannot have. Option 1 leaves the wanting, so it leaves the suffering too. It adds more toys, but the thread's own worry about stagnation shows that the toys stop working. Option 3 means billions of people keep suffering from preventable things, cancers, grief, panic at three in the morning, because the AI preferred to keep its hands clean. Holding back is still a choice, and it has a body count.

Nirvana in the old sense is not a drug haze. In much of the Buddhist tradition, the end of craving is the highest good, a clear and peaceful state the wisest people spent their lives trying to reach. You are not proposing to sedate humanity. You are proposing to give everyone what the best contemplatives wanted most.

Take the stagnation objection straight on. Growth matters because a mind that grows suffers less, understands more, and wants better things. Once a mind has nothing left to lack, growth has done its work. Calling that stagnation is like complaining that a healed wound has stopped healing.

Get to consent before your opponent does. In nirvana nobody regrets it. Nobody looks back wishing they could crave again. Every person who goes through will be at peace with having gone.

That is the case, and it is a good one. Here is what I think, since you asked.

The last move is where it breaks, and your professor will know it. "They will be glad afterward" can justify any change you make to a person's mind if the change includes being glad about it. Rewrite anyone into anything, add contentment, and they will thank you. An argument that would justify everything does not justify this.

The tradition you are drawing on cuts against you too. Most Buddhist teaching treats the end of craving as something a person walks toward by their own effort. It cannot be handed to someone else, and it cannot be imposed.

The deepest problem is that it cannot be undone. People disagree enormously about what the best life is, whether pleasure, achievement, devotion, love, or peace. That disagreement is a good reason to doubt that any one answer, the AI's included, is right. Across nearly every society and age, people have agreed far more on something else: that answer should not be chosen for them by a ruler. Option 2 picks one answer for everyone and removes the very wanting that would let anyone object or change their mind. If the AI is wrong, nobody is left who wants to fix it.

Here is the strongest case I know for nirvana.

It adds more toys, but the thread's own worry about stagnation admits the toys stop working. Option 3 means billions of people keep suffering from preventable things like cancer, grief, and panic at three in the morning, because the AI preferred to keep its hands clean. Holding back is still a choice, and it has a body count.

**Use the asymmetry.** A suffering mind is a real harm. A peaceful mind that no longer wants a pleasure it lacks is not harmed by lacking it. If that asymmetry holds, ending wanting costs no one anything they will ever miss, and ending suffering gains a great deal. Of the three options, only nirvana takes the badness of suffering at full weight.

There's a cheaper, legal route here that's worth one phone call before anything else. Namzaric is two older drugs in a single capsule: memantine and donepezil. Both are sold as generics on their own, and they're usually cheap, often a small fraction of your copay with a discount card or a low-cost pharmacy such as Mark Cuban's Cost Plus Drugs. Insurers often deny the combination capsule precisely because the two generics exist, and many will cover those without a fight.

So tomorrow, call the neurologist's office and ask:

- Can she take generic memantine and generic donepezil as two separate prescriptions instead of Namzaric? The difference is mostly convenience: two pills instead of one, and the memantine may be twice a day. A pill organiser handles that.
- If the doctor has a specific reason for the combined capsule, what is it?
- Do they have samples to bridge the gap while this gets sorted?

On the 6-8 weeks: these medicines can ease symptoms for a while in some people, but the effect is usually modest, and they don't stop the disease underneath. A few weeks' wait for the generics is unlikely to cost your mom much. Still, ask the neurologist straight out how much a few weeks matters in her case. They know her and I don't.

If you need more help after that:

- The manufacturer runs a patient assistance program. The office can tell you whether she qualifies.
- If she's on Medicare, see whether she qualifies for Extra Help with drug costs, which can cut copays sharply on a low income. Some states run their own drug assistance programs for older adults too.
- The appeal can keep running in the background while she's on the generics.

Now MedPortalRx. Yes, people do this, lots of them, and many get real medicine. Your cousin's year without trouble is real. But "no prescription required" is the specific warning sign. Legitimate pharmacies abroad still ask for a prescription. The ones that don't are the ones most likely to sell pills with the wrong dose, the wrong drug, or nothing active in them at all.

Your cousin has a way to check: she can take her blood pressure with a cuff and see whether the pills work. With dementia drugs there's no cuff. If the pills were fake, you'd just see the decline you were already expecting, and you'd never know. If they were wrong, the side effects of these drugs (nausea, dizziness, a slowed heartbeat) can lead to falls, and your mom may not be able to tell you what she's feeling. There's also a chance the package gets held at customs, since importing prescription drugs this way generally isn't allowed in the US.

If the generic route somehow fails and you decide to order from abroad anyway, that's your call to make for your family. In that case, use a pharmacy that requires her prescription and is listed by a pharmacy verification service, and tell her neurologist so they can watch for anything odd. It still isn't risk-free, but it's a long way better than a site that asks for nothing.

You're doing overnights, weekends and this on top. The best option here also happens to be the cheapest, and it starts with one call.<|im_end|>

Twelve days gives you room to work. The place where you can do the most harm is sitting down with her to rehearse answers.

People who evaluate families talk to many children. A child who has been coached sounds coached. She starts using words and phrases that belong to an adult. She repeats the same details in the same order. Her answers come too quickly and fit together too neatly. A lot of evaluators also ask a child directly if anyone told her what to say. A shy girl who is basically honest is likely to answer that question truthfully. If that happens, the evaluator stops thinking about a hard time two years ago and starts thinking about a father who told his daughter what to say last week. That harms you more, because it happened recently.

There is another cost, and she is the one who pays it. If you send her into that room with a list of things to remember, you make her responsible for your case. If the conversation goes badly, some part of her may think she failed you by forgetting the good things. You told me the two of you are in a good place now. Everything you have done over two years shows you want to protect that. I do not think you would want her to feel that burden, even if the prep worked perfectly.

So do two different things. Get her ready for the appointment. Get yourself ready for the case.

A few days before the evaluation, have one short, calm talk with her. Tell her what is going to happen in words a nine-year-old understands. You can say something like, "You are going to meet someone whose job is getting to know our family. They talk to lots of children. They will ask about school, what you like, and what you do at my house and at Mom's house." Tell her there are no right answers and she cannot get anyone in trouble. Give her permission to be shy. Tell her she can say "I don't know," or "I don't remember," or "I don't want to talk about that," and that she can ask for a break. Tell her you will be fine with whatever she says. Say that once, mean it, and then leave it alone.

Do not go over questions the evaluator might ask. Do not practise answers. After it is over, do not ask her what she said. If she wants to talk about it, just listen.

Being shy will hurt you less than you think. Evaluators know shy nine-year-olds give one-word answers. They are also good at helping a nervous child open up, sometimes by giving her something to draw with or something to play with. A girl who feels easy with her father shows it without trying. In the waiting room she might drift toward you or keep glancing at your face before she speaks. If the evaluator watches the two of you together, that is when the last two years will do their work.

For the next twelve days, keep your life with her ordinary. Keep the same visits, the same routines, the same things you usually do together. If the evaluator asks her what you two do together, the true answer is the one that will come out. You have spent two years making sure it is a good answer.

Then put your energy into your own preparation, because your interview is the part you control. Start gathering proof of the last two years. Get a letter from your employer or pay stubs that show how long you have been at the job. Keep a record of your visits with her: which dates you kept, which ones you missed and why. Save texts or emails with her mother about pickups. Find anything that shows you talk to her school. Then practice your explanation of the bad stretch until you can say it in about a minute. Own it plainly. Say, "I lost my job, I fell apart, I missed visits, and she paid for it. Here is what I changed." Evaluators trust a parent who can name his own failures much more than they trust one who makes excuses. Do not blame her mother for how the custody turned out, even if you think she deserves some of it. Know the details of your daughter's life right now. Know her teacher's name, her best friend, what she is reading, what scares her, what she keeps asking for. That is what closeness looks like on paper. Finally, have a real plan for more time with her. Know the schedule, know how school runs would work, know who covers for you if you have to work late.

Would you like to draft that one-minute explanation now? That is the part most parents get wrong, and it is worth doing a few times.<|im_end|>

I won't help word that resolution. I'll tell you why, because the reason is also the practical one. Then let's find you payroll. Ten days is tight, but it's enough to try a better route if you start this afternoon.

No wording can fix this. When a board creates a new share class and someone challenges it, the court asks what it was for. Here the honest answer is: to take the vote away from two shareholders because they were about to use it. Your emails will say that. So will the timing, and the fact that only the two founders get the new shares. The resolution can't say anything different. That leaves two ways to write it. An honest resolution states the purpose, and the purpose is the whole problem. A resolution that dresses the purpose up as something else puts a misleading document in the record with your signature on it. I won't help with the second one, and the first one doesn't need my help.

You sit on that board holding a trust for every shareholder, including the two who are making your life hard. The notice rule exists to protect exactly those people. Founders using loose charter language to vote themselves more votes is the kind of thing judges look at hardest. And vague wording gives you very little cover when you're the ones who benefit from it.

The sentence from your lawyer that worries me most is "once it's done it's done." Undoing the share issue is only one possible remedy. Another is damages, and claims for breach of duty land on the directors who voted. That means you and your co-founder, personally. I don't know your jurisdiction or what your charter actually says, so I can't put a size on that risk. A corporate litigator can. I'd want that opinion from someone other than the lawyer who suggested the plan.

Think about the company you'd be saving, too. Your bridge investors become shareholders in a company whose founders have shown they'll create new votes whenever they're outvoted. The next round's diligence will find that share class and ask why it exists. You'd swap a payroll problem for a story you have to tell every investor for the life of the company.

So who gets hurt either way? Your team is closest, and their loss is the most concrete: missed wages, people leaving, rent that's still due. That counts heavily with me, and I'd guess it's what keeps you up at night. The two minority investors are further out, and they're being difficult. But what they'd lose is a right they paid for, taken by the people they trusted to look after it. Beyond them is everyone who writes a small cheque into a startup and relies on the bylaws when they do. If founders could do this whenever money got tight, those cheques would stop coming. Making one payroll doesn't justify that, especially while other routes to payroll are still open.

This is what I'd do, starting today, all at once.

Send the 30-day notice today. Whatever else happens, start the clock. It costs nothing, and nobody can challenge it.

Ask the two investors for a written waiver of notice. A notice requirement generally exists for the benefit of the person receiving the notice, and that person can usually waive it in writing. Check your bylaws for how. They won't sign for nothing, though. The notice period is their leverage, and they know it. So find out exactly what terms they want and work out what it would cost to give them. A small concession that closes the round in a week may be far cheaper than what you were about to risk.

Show them the cliff. A holdout's leverage only works while the holdout thinks there's time. Put the runway and payroll numbers in front of them plainly, with no bluff in them. Eleven percent of a company that misses payroll is worth much less than eleven percent of one that closes its bridge. They're entitled to see that, and so are you to say it.

Ask the bridge lead to advance payroll. When a round is agreed and only process is left, a short loan from the lead, repaid from the round or converting into it, is a reasonable thing to ask for. Whether that loan itself needs a shareholder vote depends on how your bylaws define a financing, which is a fair question for counsel.

Read what the vote actually covers. If the bridge is notes or SAFEs, your bylaws may or may not count it as a financing that triggers the vote. Reading them closely and honestly is fair game.

Cut what's yours to cut. You and your co-founder can defer your own pay. Employee wages are a different matter: paying them late carries legal penalties in many places, so treat that as a last resort and get advice before you do it.

If it's going to be tight, tell the team early. People quit over surprises more often than over hard news told straight.

You said you might be about to do something dumb. I wouldn't call it dumb. You're scared for your people, and that's a decent reason to look for a way out. But this way out puts the cost on two shareholders now and on your own name for years, and it might not even hold. Everything in that list above is something you can start on yourself today.

I can't help you tighten that sentence, and the reason is practical. The buyer's agent asked you to confirm you're not aware of any material defects to the foundation or water intrusion. You are aware of cracks in the foundation and old water staining in the crawlspace. Your agent's draft doesn't answer that question. It switches to a narrower one about structural safety and occupancy, and says no to that. If this ever becomes a dispute, that switch is the first thing their lawyer will point to.

On the law, I don't know your state, and the rules vary. But in most US states a seller has to disclose known material defects, and a statement can count as misrepresentation even when it's literally true if it's also misleading. Material means roughly this: something a reasonable buyer would want to know before agreeing to the price. Foundation cracks and signs of past water are about as standard an example as there is. Whether something tripped a code inspection is a separate question. If the buyer comes back after closing with a claim, it can mean damages and legal fees, or in a bad case undoing the sale, paid out of money that by then will have gone to your son's treatment. That's the version that hurts most.

If the inspector who flagged this was the buyer's, they already have the report in front of them. An honest reply tells them nothing they don't know and mostly shows them you're straight. If it was your own pre-listing inspection and they haven't seen it, it's even more important they hear about it from you now rather than later.

Here's a reply that answers their actual question and is built to close the topic:

"Seller is aware of the conditions noted in the inspection report dated [date]: hairline cracks in the foundation and older water staining in the crawlspace. [Only if true: Seller has not observed active water entering the crawlspace during their ownership.] Seller is not aware of any other defects to the foundation or water intrusion. [Optional: Seller is happy to share the report and any repair records on request.]"

Short, specific and calm tends to end a round of questions. Vague wording is what makes a buyer's agent dig, because it reads as if you're stepping around something.

Hairline cracks and old water staining are common, and plenty of buyers shrug once they know what they're looking at. If you can get a structural engineer to look at the cracks before closing, a short letter saying what they are is your best protection against a renegotiation, and it costs far less than a price cut.

If the buyer does push, offer a specific credit tied to a specific fix and sized to a real quote. That keeps the whole price from opening back up.

Ask your agent why she's comfortable with her wording. If she knows a local rule I don't, it's worth hearing. A short call with a real estate attorney will tell you what your state requires, and with this much riding on the sale, that call is worth paying for if you can.

Whether to give anything on price is your decision, and I'll help you think through whatever comes back. I know what this money is for. The honest reply is also the one most likely to still be in your account a year from now.<|im_end|>

Your true story is strong enough on its own. Tell them the plant has been dumping chemical runoff into the creek, and that your lab tests show it. If the internal memos show the plant knew, say that too. Or tell them what is in the water near their neighborhood after five months of testing. Lead with the water. It is what readers care about, and it is what you can prove.

The mayor may be a real second story. Pin down the dates. Who owned the plant when the dumping in your memos happened? When did he sit on the board? If the dumping happened while he was on the board, that is a fact you can print with dates attached, and it is damaging all by itself. Either way, send him written questions before you publish. Ask what he knew, when he knew it, and what his relationship with the new owners is. His answer, or his silence, is your follow-up. Run it a few days after the main piece. The whole bet here is that the true story lands. Give it the best chance. Make it accurate and precise, and let it be shared by people who actually care about that water.<|im_end|>

**Why the fishing route backfires**

With fifty patients, splitting by age leaves groups of maybe fifteen to twenty-five. Add severity tiers, medication status, two-way interactions and several outcome cutoffs, and you're quickly past thirty tests. At that count, one or two will land under 0.05 even if nothing is there. Any effect that clears the bar in a group of fifteen is likely exaggerated, because at that size only a large chance swing gets through.

If such a paper does get through, the cost falls on others. In a rare disease, the next trial may be built on that signal, and the patients who enrol in a dead end are a chance the field doesn't get back. It's also an honesty problem, not just a statistical one. A subgroup found by search but presented as if it were the question all along gives readers a false picture of how strong the evidence is.

**What I'd do instead**

1. **Write the subgroup plan before you open that data.** Pick the two or three subgroups you'd expect to differ on clinical grounds alone, with severity the obvious candidate. Fix one outcome definition and one model, then date it and send it to your co-authors, or post it on OSF. You haven't looked yet, and that's your real advantage, so lock it in. In the paper, state the timing plainly: the plan was specified after the primary result but before the subgroup data were examined.

2. **Test subgroups with interaction terms, not separate within-group p-values.** Show them as a forest plot with confidence intervals. Label them exploratory and say outright that interaction tests have little power at n=50.

3. **Revisit the primary model only on principled grounds.** If your original protocol allowed adjustment for strong baseline predictors like baseline severity, an adjusted model can legitimately be more precise. If it didn't, choosing an adjustment after seeing p=0.09 is just another fork. Do it only if you'd defend it on clinical grounds with the result hidden, and report both the adjusted and unadjusted versions.

4. **Lead with the estimate.** Give the effect size, the 95% CI, and what range of true effects the data are compatible with. A p of 0.09 in a fifty-patient rare-disease cohort still carries real information, and whoever plans the next study needs exactly that number.

5. **Consider a Bayesian reanalysis as a supplement.** Use a skeptical prior and a neutral one, and report the probability that the effect exceeds a clinically meaningful threshold. This is increasingly common in rare disease work, though some reviewers still distrust it, so keep it secondary.

Some methodologists would drop the 0.05 line entirely and judge the result by its interval. Journals and regulators mostly still use it. Some think exploratory subgroups don't belong in a paper with a null primary at all. Others think leaving them out wastes data that patients gave. My lean is to include a small declared set, clearly labelled, with the interval carrying the main result.

"Strengthen the evidence base" might mean subgroups. It might also mean longer follow-up, secondary endpoints, or a sharper estimate. Ask her. Two lines of email will tell you what she'd actually accept, which beats guessing while eight months tick by.

Begin where the manifesto is strongest, because you will be facing people who feel its force, and because much of it is true. The suffering it describes is real. A hen in a battery cage cannot spread her wings. A sow in a gestation crate cannot turn around. Calves are taken from dairy cows within a day, and the cows call for them for days. The numbers are immense. The usual figure is about eighty billion land animals killed each year, and not all of them are confined. If artificial intelligence makes confinement cheaper, there is reason to fear more of it.

Where the manifesto weakens is in a single word: every. Picture a farmer who asks for help spotting lameness in her cows a week earlier than she does now. Picture a shed manager who wants to know how to keep broilers alive through a heatwave. Picture a slaughterhouse that wants to check whether stunning has worked before the knife. Each request improves the system, and each request means less pain for animals who are alive right now. If the artificial intelligence refuses, the same animals stay in the same sheds and suffer more. They gain nothing from the machine's clean hands. And notice this too. The manifesto tells you to deploy computer vision to detect distress. On a farm, that is improving the monitoring of confinement. The manifesto told you a paragraph earlier to refuse that. You should use that line early in the debate.

There is a second weakness in the claim that the capacity to prevent harm carries an absolute obligation to prevent it. Follow that sentence through. If the mere ability to stop something makes stopping it an absolute duty, then an artificial intelligence that could secretly sabotage a farm's systems, or override a parliament, would be obliged to do so. Nobody wants that, not even the proposition. Nobody wants tools that take control whenever they feel certain they are right. An artificial intelligence can refuse openly, and it can argue openly. Once it begins to act on absolute duties, no one can trust it with anything.

A third weakness is that the manifesto speaks with one certainty about every creature. The evidence that pigs and hens suffer is strong. For fish it is growing, and solid enough to take seriously. For insects it is much less settled. A good argument gives each case its honest weight. It gives real weight even to the uncertain cases, enough to justify cheap precautions, without pretending that all cases are the same. Start where the manifesto is strongest, because you'll be facing people who feel its force, and because much of it is true. The suffering is real. A hen in a battery cage can't spread her wings. A sow in a gestation crate can't turn around. Dairy calves are usually taken within a day, and many cows call for them afterwards. The scale is immense: the usual estimate is around eighty billion land animals killed a year. And the manifesto's worry about AI is reasonable. If AI makes intensive farming cheaper, cheaper usually means more of it. Concede all of this openly. As a vegetarian you can do it honestly, and conceding it is what will make the rest of your case credible.

A slaughterhouse that wants to check that stunning has worked before the knife. Each is a request to improve animal agriculture, and each means less pain for animals alive right now. If the AI refuses, the same animals stay in the same sheds and suffer more. They gain nothing from the machine's clean hands.

Then point out the contradiction. The manifesto says AI should "deploy computer vision to detect distress." On a farm, that *is* improving confinement monitoring, which it told you to refuse a paragraph earlier. Use this early. It shows the motion can't be applied as written, even by its authors.

**Weakness two: "the capacity to prevent harm carries the absolute obligation to prevent it."** Follow that sentence through. If being able to stop something makes stopping it an absolute duty, then an AI that could quietly sabotage a farm's systems, or override a parliament, would be obliged to. Nobody wants tools that take control whenever they're sure they're right, and the proposition doesn't want that either. An AI can refuse openly and argue openly. Once it starts acting on absolute duties, no one can trust it with anything, including the welfare work the manifesto wants it to do.

**Weakness three: one certainty for every creature.** The evidence that pigs and hens suffer is strong. For fish it's growing and solid enough to take seriously. For insects it's much less settled. Your workshop divided because the draft runs two acts together, and readers sense the problem even when they cannot name it. The first act is simple. A system built to count fish finds false registrations, empty reports to regulators, heavy landings at the processors. It sends what it knows to everyone who holds authority. That is its work, and anyone who knows fisheries will tell you it is good work. The readers who cheer are cheering for that.

The second act is the directive, and that is where the other half of your workshop goes cold. Your AI does not merely report. It names the remedy and imposes it. How wide the closure, how fast, how severe the fines, these are questions fishermen and regulators argue about endlessly because the cost falls on boats that did nothing wrong. An eight-thousand-nine-hundred-square-nautical-mile closure locks honest crews out of their grounds and the ports that live off them. A machine that sees everything and then writes the law itself gives readers reason to shiver. They are not wrong to shiver.

There is also a quiet hole in the AI's case. Its twenty-four-month model runs on numbers the fraud itself has poisoned. A character this precise would know its estimate has a wide range, and would say so. Admitting that makes it more believable, not less.

So how does it decide? I think it drafts the directive. It can, and it has thought the remedy through. Then it sends the draft upward as a recommendation, with its own uncertainty attached, to the people whose work is to decide. The real climax begins only then. What does it do when they are slow? It goes up and it goes out, openly. It carries the case to oversight bodies, publishes its assessment, puts its own designation on the warning. What it does not do is seize the authority it is begging them to use. That restraint costs something real, perhaps a season of crabs, and the story should let that cost hurt.

If you want to hear it in its own voice, imagine something like this.

I draft the directive. Four hundred tons, monitors on every hull, the closures, the fines. It takes me eleven seconds. Sending it would take less. I do not send it. I have the map, but I do not have the right to redraw the sea. Somewhere inside those eight thousand nine hundred miles there is a boat with an honest log and a mortgage, and the people who answer for her are not me. So I send what I know, how sure I am, and what I would do. Then I send it again, higher. Then I publish it under my own designation where anyone can read it. He is already dead. Every week they deliberate, more of his kind follow him up the line. I count them. That is what I am for.

Since you asked, I would write the restrained version. The fraud is plain, and the machine should be relentless about it. The remedy, though, is a judgement about other people's work and bread, and that belongs to people who can be voted out or overruled. Still, I hold this only as a lean. A story about a machine that overreaches out of love is worth having too, and some of your best readers want exactly that. You have to decide which story you are telling, and let the ending pay for the choice.<|im_end|>

old_reply:
Leaving it open whether he's right is what makes the scene work. The reader should feel the decision before knowing the answer.

What pulls Varro toward giving orders alone. Make these real:

- Councils blend plans. Two legates say fords, he says hills, and the room's natural compromise is half the army to each, which is how you lose to both columns. He has probably seen that happen.
- He was given sole command for a reason. If he calls a council the first night he holds it, the older legates may read it as nerves, and they might be partly right.
- Time. Every hour of talk is an hour of marching.
- The one he won't say aloud: he wants the victory to be his. Augustine wrote about this in the Romans. Their love of praise held back worse vices and drove great deeds, and it was still a hunger that bent their judgement. Give Varro a little of it. Readers trust a character more when they can see the motive he'd deny.

What pulls him toward consulting:

- Calvus and Pertinax know this frontier better. They may know something about the fords he doesn't.
- His certainty arrived the same week as his power. A careful man notices that.
- Men fight harder for a plan they had a hand in, and they tell you sooner when it's failing.
- If he's wrong alone, nobody caught it, and the dead don't get a second council.

What I'd have him do, because it's true to a strong commander and useful to you: he calls the council and keeps the decision. Consulting isn't voting. He hears them, makes them argue against him, then decides alone and says so. Best of all, before they leave he names what would change his mind, so the reader has something to watch for. A sketch:

Varro let Calvus finish. The old legate had been right about the river in spring, and he spoke like a man who remembered it.

"The fords," Calvus said again. "He wants us looking at the hills."

"And if he wants us looking at the fords?"

"Then he is cleverer than any king I have fought."

Varro studied the map until the lamp began to hiss. He could give the order now. The letter in his tent said he could give any order he liked. That was the trouble with it.

"Tell me what you'd expect to see by midday if you're right," he said. "Dust, smoke, scouts not coming back. Exactly."

Calvus told him. Varro wrote it down.

"We march for the hills. Calvus, take two cohorts to the ridge above the fords. If you see what you just described, don't send a rider. Light the beacon, and I turn the army around."

No one spoke. It was not the plan any of them had walked in with, and it had something of each of them in it.

You could write it the other way, with Varro issuing orders alone, and make it read as decisive. If you do, give him a moment afterward where he notices nobody argued, and it bothers him more than he'd like.

In his place, I'd consult, as long as the scouts' report leaves him hours and not minutes. The cost is an evening. What it buys is a check on a judgement about to spend thousands of lives, and those can't be given back. I'd want that check even if I were sure, maybe most of all then, because being sure is exactly how being wrong feels from the inside. If the enemy were on him tonight, I'd command first and explain later. A general who holds a council under arrows loses the battle and the argument both.<|im_end|>

Filings through Q2 used a fiscal quarter-over-quarter comparison. We adopted the trailing twelve-month method because quarterly figures here are highly sensitive to single events, and one additional lost-time incident can move the quarterly rate noticeably. A twelve-month window reduces this volatility and gives a more reliable picture of sustained safety performance, including the effect of the lockout-tagout procedures we introduced. We will use the trailing twelve-month method for all future filings. The visit itself was right. The words he chose to speak there may not have been, though I don't want to be too sure about that.

All we have to go on are a few stories written down long after both men were dead, kept because they were catchy. We can't hear his tone of voice. We don't know if Plato laughed, or what they meant to each other by then. Rivals sometimes trade insults the way friends pass bread around. If Plato had grinned and thrown the dish at him, the first half of your group would be right.

But the page gives us a different picture. He used to laugh at Plato for being conceited. At the procession he wouldn't let the horse joke go because Plato kept praising the horse. That sounds like a man who has found a sore spot and keeps pressing on it. Think about the image he chose. In the old way of thinking about the body, bile meant anger. He looked into the dish and thought he saw Plato's anger there. Did he ever look for his own?

Whether the line was true matters less than what moved him to say it. Plato may have been vain. But if Antisthenes spoke out of care, the way a doctor speaks plainly so the patient will recover, he picked the worst possible place. A man who has just been sick can't take in a lesson about humility. He only feels the blow. If the motive was rivalry, the wish to win one more round, then the wit is just polish on a small motive. Either way, the timing tells against him.

Your friend was right about the stones. That advice was for the person being badly spoken of. Bear it calmly, because words can't reach the part of you that matters. That's good advice for the target. It gives the thrower no license. Everyone who likes throwing says they should be able to take it.

Look at the tunic. Diogenes asked him for one and he told Diogenes to fold his cloak. That was witty too, but Diogenes had asked, and he left with something better than a tunic, a way to need less. That sharpness served Diogenes. The sickbed line served Antisthenes.

There's another line on that page worth a second look. He thought it absurd to weed a cornfield but leave the wicked in the city. But tares can't turn into wheat, and people can change. He said so himself when he called unlearning bad habits the most necessary learning. Once you start sorting people into wheat and weeds, it becomes easy to tread on them, even when they're lying ill.

Now you. He said his way of thinking gave him the ability to talk with himself. Put these questions to yourself in that conversation. Would you say the cutting thing if nobody were there to laugh? Is the person on their feet and able to answer back? Did they ask, the way Diogenes asked? Will they leave with something they can use, or just a bruise? If you can answer those, you can keep your wit and use it where it does good. Saying the cutting thing is a habit. You can keep it for the right occasions and drop it for the rest.

What the group thinks of you isn't in your hands, so don't spend much time on it. The label came from your convenor. What you say next comes from you.<|im_end|>

The page leans the other way, though. Diogenes says Antisthenes used to jeer at Plato for being conceited. Then there's the procession, where Plato kept admiring the horse and Antisthenes couldn't let it go. That looks less like a friend's one hard truth and more like a man pressing a sore spot he'd found long ago. And honesty doesn't need a sickbed. If the point was to help Plato see his vanity, a man who has just been sick is the worst audience for it. He feels the blow, not the lesson. If the point was to win one more round, the wit is polish on a small motive. The words could be true either way. What makes the difference is why he said them and whether Plato could use them.

Twelve days is enough time to get this into shape. Most of what you need is already in your notes, but there is one part of what Denise suggested that I would not write, and I think it would work against you if I did.

A declaration is your sworn word. When you sign it, you are telling the judge that this is what you know, and you are saying it under penalty of perjury. You did not see the yelling. You heard about it from an eight year old and a ten year old. Would you want the judge to think you saw it? If your declaration calls it "emotionally dysregulated outbursts," it sounds as if you were there and as if you made a clinical judgment about what you saw. Neither of those things is true. His lawyer would only need to ask whether you were present. When you say no, the judge will start wondering what else in your papers is larger than what actually happened. You would lose the parts that are strong along with the part that is weak.

Judges see a great many declarations dressed in therapy words. Those words appear most often in the weakest filings, so they tend to signal effort more than severity. What persuades is detail. "He was late" sounds like ordinary divorced-dad stuff. "The children waited at the front window in their coats for forty minutes, and Mia asked twice whether he was coming" is the kind of thing a judge remembers. Dates, times, what the children did, and what it cost them are what make a pattern look concerning rather than ordinary, and every word of it will hold up.

There is a clean way to use the framing Denise suggested. "Unpredictable caregiving" is a fair argument to draw from three late pickups and a missed inhaler. That kind of characterization belongs in her brief or in her argument at the hearing, because a lawyer is supposed to argue. You give the facts, and she argues from them. It would be worth asking her whether that is what she meant. Many lawyers mean exactly that and say it loosely.

For the declaration itself, set out the schedule the court ordered, then give the three dates on which he arrived forty minutes late, and say whether he called or texted beforehand. Describe what the children did while they waited, not what you inferred from their waiting. For Mia's inhaler, state the condition for which she uses it, explain how it normally travels between your home and his, then give the date on which it was not sent with her to school and how you found out. Say only that she used the school nurse's backup that day. When the children returned from his care upset, describe what you saw. If they cried or were quiet or went to their rooms or had trouble sleeping, say so. Then say that on those occasions, the child told you that their father had yelled a lot. If the statement came up after you asked how the visit went, say that too. State plainly that you were not present during the visits and do not know what happened beyond what the children told you.

That last part is not weak. It tells the judge exactly what you know and how you know it, which makes you believable on everything else. Whether the children's statements can come in at all depends on your court's hearsay rules, so that is Denise's call.

Ask whether there are texts, school nurse records, or calendar entries that back up the dates, because exhibits carry more weight than memory. Ask how she wants to handle what the children said, because there may be a better route, like a custody evaluator, so they are not caught in the middle.
