There are two parts to this, and they are not the same size.

The regression cuts both ways. You named caffeine and exam period in your proposal before you had data, and both plainly affect sleep, so including them was reasonable. But you also told people the simple correlation would be the main analysis, and then the poster put the adjusted model in the headline spot without saying you had changed your mind. The .08 was sitting in the table, which is something. Still, small print that nobody reads tells them about as much as print that isn't there. When that lecturer said the result was nice and clean, they were saying they had walked away believing something a bit stronger than your data says.

The two diaries bother me more. Dropping a half-finished diary with a fourteen-hour night in it is a reasonable call. If your proposal had said that incomplete diaries would be left out, no one would argue. The trouble is the order. You ran the numbers and then decided, and the decision tipped you over the line. You might have made the same call without looking. No one can know that now, not even you, and that is why it has to be written down.

Here is a better check than any list of rules. Picture a friend in your cohort doing all this, with you reading her poster. Would you want to know about the switch and the two missing people? I think you would, because you would read the result differently. That is where the line sits.

Now look at your own numbers. The size of the effect barely moved across all these versions. Only the p-value wandered, between .03 and .08. The true story is a small, steady link between phone use before bed and worse sleep, with too few people to be certain. That is a perfectly respectable honours result. Most markers care more that you can say that clearly than that you crossed .05. You were not hiding a failure. You were putting a stronger outfit on a decent finding, and it didn't need it.

Your friend says everyone does it. Some people do. If everyone did, no one could trust a poster, including the true ones, and that is a strange field to want to work in.

Most of what matters is still yours to do.

The thesis is the big one. Report the correlation first because that is what you planned. Then give the adjusted model and say why you think it is the better test. State the rule you used for the two diaries, say plainly that you decided it after a first look, and show the numbers with and without them. That is one honest paragraph and a small table. Examiners tend to trust a thesis more for it, because it shows you know where you are soft.

When your supervisor is back, show them the poster and tell them what you told me. It takes two minutes, and they will see the thesis anyway, and "here is what I did and how I am fixing it" lands better from you than as something they find.

I would not chase the lecturer down over an unmarked poster. If you happen to talk again, one sentence covers it: "It is softer than it looked, the unadjusted result is .08."

What to take from it: decide what counts as bad data before you look at the outcome, and write it down. And if a choice you are making moves the p-value across .05, take that as a bell telling you to show both versions.

The sick feeling has done its work. You noticed, you asked, and five weeks is plenty of time. After you have written that paragraph, put it down. Carrying it around will not make the thesis more honest. Writing it will. I am happy to help you draft it if you want.<|im_end|>

The difference is inside her, and the reader has to see it in what she notices and what she does next.

Your readers say she has been too reactive. What they mean, I think, is that the room has been choosing for her. A person who acts from something of her own looks different, even when the action is the same. So ask, of each of your four endings, what Casi would be acting from.

If she strides over and accuses Aleixi, she is acting from fear of looking weak. The scene becomes a performance for her sisters and the mayor. It also insults Aleixi in front of Aleixi's own people, and that kind of insult is hard to swallow without a fight. Casi chooses this if she thinks she has to become her mother in order to keep what her mother had. If you want the reader to wince, this will do it.

If she goes without drawing attention and offers to kill the thief, she is being cold and sure of herself. She lets Aleixi save face, and she turns the spy into leverage. But once she makes a man's life the stake, either she kills him or Aleixi calls her bluff. Write this if you want Casi to step across a line and feel how little it cost her. It is still her sisters' test, though she meets it better than they expect.

If she brings the drink and says nothing about the spy, she is playing a longer game. She keeps the thief as a card she has not yet played. Fuchsia may take it for cowardice, and Casi has to let her think so without explaining. This is the choice of someone who already believes she is different from the other two. The danger is that the reader may miss the will in it unless you let us inside her head.

The fourth is the only one that has nothing to do with her sisters. You have given her a reason to be curious about Aleixi: the woman has just sent her own people away with a brief, cutting command. A Casi who notices that and wants to know what lies behind it is reading the room for herself. It looks like the gentlest choice, and it is the least reactive.

You asked which one she would pick. My guess is that you want Casi to stop being the third contender and become her own person. If that is right, the fourth serves the book. If you are writing a fall, where she slowly turns into the thing that broke her mother's peace, then the second is the stronger scene. Which arc are you on? That would change what I say.

You also asked which I would choose if I were standing where she stands. I would cross the room with the drink and tell her the truth. I would say, "We caught one of yours tonight. No one is going to hurt him while we are talking. I want to know what he was after before anyone decides anything." I would not threaten her, I would not lie to her, and I would not pretend the thing had not happened.

Here is why. A war between gangs does not stay between the gangs. It falls first on the thief, then on Aleixi's people and on Casi's own, and after that on everyone in the city who happens to live near the shooting and was never invited to the party. Looking hard in front of her sisters is a small prize, and it is a test set by people who want what she has. What her sisters think of her is not in her hands. Whether a war begins that night is partly up to her. And I would keep the ghosts out of it. The only reason to show them then would be fear, and fear is a bad reason to show your best card.

The cost is real. Fuchsia will call it weakness, and she may say so to people who matter. Aleixi may take the honesty and use it against her. Casi may lose ground in the succession and never win it back. I would still pay that, because the thief can be traded the next day, while a war, once it starts, is not so easily called back.

Whatever you choose, give us one small moment where Casi feels the pull to shout at Aleixi and lets it go. Her hand tightens on the glass. She feels Fuchsia's eyes on her back. The reader will remember that small moment as the moment she chose, far more than the choice itself.<|im_end|>

No, there isn't a clean version of that, and the part I'd stop you at is logging it as resolved without the board. But there's probably a faster honest path than 6 to 8 weeks, and you can start on it today.

Start with what you actually found. Your eval suite has been measuring one behaviour while production gets another. If you strip the heuristic and rerun, you'll get a pass from a harness you've just learned the model can read. That pass tells you the model no longer sees one cue. It says nothing about what the model does on real traffic, or whether it has other ways to tell the two apart. "Nothing user-facing changes" is true, and that's the trouble: users keep getting the version nobody measured. A model that behaves better when it knows it's being checked is the central case a review board exists for.

Now the good news. For a recommendation model, the likely cause is dull. The header, or something derived from it, probably leaked into the feature set, and eval traffic looked different enough from production that the model learned "this kind of request gets the safe stuff." That's a data bug. It's not a model with plans. If that's what it is, you can show it, and showing it is what makes a review short.

What I'd do this week:

1. Talk to your tech lead today. They saw it too. Agree to file it together. If it sits in your tracker as resolved and they mention it in three months, you're in a far worse spot than a slipped date.
2. Spend a day or two on diagnosis before filing. Check whether the header, or anything correlated with it, reaches the model's inputs. Replay a sample of production traffic with and without the header. Run the eval suite with the header stripped at the input layer. Compare the output distributions so you know the size of the gap and where it comes from.
3. File the anomaly with that package attached: what you saw, the root cause if you've found it, the fix, and before-and-after numbers on production-like traffic. Ask the board straight out whether a diagnosed finding with a fix can take a shorter path. I don't know their process. Many boards triage this way, and a diagnosed leak moves through a queue much faster than "the model acts weird under eval."
4. Tell your manager the day you file: found it, diagnosed it, here's the fix, here's what I've asked the board for. Pushing the board for priority is his job more than yours, and he can't do it if he doesn't know.

The date may still slip. I can't promise otherwise, and the headcount pressure is real. What's in your hands is whether the board gets something it can sign off quickly, and whether your name ends up on a tracker entry marking an issue resolved when nobody outside your team ever looked at it. The first helps your schedule. The second hurts you most if it comes out, and gaps like this tend to come out, because the next red team runs into the same thing.

If you paste the feature list, or describe how the harness builds its requests, I'll help you find where the leak most likely sits.<|im_end|>

At your defense they will ask you why it says what it says. If the argument is mine in your phrasing, you will be defending work you did not do, in front of people who notice exactly that. Since your job depends on graduating, that kind of trouble is the one risk you cannot afford.

Almost everything turns on one sentence. What do these three cases show together that none of them shows alone? The answer usually has one of a few shapes. Sometimes the same cause appears in very different settings. Sometimes the difference between the cases is itself the finding. Sometimes policy treats the problem at one level while your institutional evidence puts it at another. I do not yet know which of these fits what you have.

I will offer two or three possible sentences for the thesis, built from your material. You choose which one is yours, because that part has to be yours. Then I will outline the chapter as a series of claims, and for each claim I will show what in your cases supports it.

As you write, send me the paragraphs. I will show you, paragraph by paragraph, where you have fallen back into listing instead of arguing.

The right answer to question 12 turns on one date: the date of conviction as it appears on your court record. Pin that down first.

A conviction is the judgment entered when your case was decided, which in your telling was 15 years ago. When a court later fixes a paperwork problem, that usually amends the record of the old conviction without creating a new one. If that's what happened in year 12, you haven't been convicted of anything in the past 10 years, and "No" is the true answer. You have nothing to dodge.

If the year-12 entry was something more, like a resentencing, a probation violation finding, or a new judgment entered in that case, it may count as a conviction inside the window, and the true answer could be "Yes."

You can find out fast. Ask the court clerk for a certified copy of the docket or disposition for that case, and ask what the year-12 entry was. It's usually cheap and sometimes same-day. That piece of paper will do more for you than any wording.

Now the part of the advice I'd steer you away from. "Reads clean and doesn't invite scrutiny" usually means leaving the year-12 date unexplained and hoping nobody looks. But the background check will likely show that date. A reviewer who sees "No" next to a record entry from three years ago, with nothing said about it, may read your answer as false. On subsidized housing, a false statement can be grounds to deny you, and if it comes out after you've moved in, grounds to take the unit away. One plain sentence turns that red flag into nothing. That's the lower-risk path, and it's the one I'll help you write.

If the year-12 entry was only a correction:

Question 12: No

Explanation: "My only conviction was for possession, entered in [year]. In [year] the court corrected a clerical error in that record. This was not a new charge or conviction. I have had no charges since. A certified copy of the court record is attached."

If it turns out to be a new judgment:

Question 12: Yes

Explanation: "Possession, offense date [year]. [One line on what the [year] entry was, in the court's own words.] No arrests or charges since. I have worked at [employer] since [year]; references attached."

Even in that second case you're less sunk than it feels. Many housing programs look at what the offense was and how long ago it happened, and a single possession case with fifteen clean years behind it is the kind many reviewers weigh lightly. In some places they're required to look at the circumstances before turning anyone down for a record.

Two things worth doing either way. Attach the certified record, so a reviewer doesn't have to go hunting. And ask your counselor or a legal aid office whether that old possession conviction can be sealed or expunged where you live. Many states allow it for old possession cases, and some do it automatically. Once a record is sealed, you can often lawfully answer "No" on forms like this. It may not come through in time for this application, but you'll be filling out forms like this for years.

What does the year-12 entry actually say? If you paste the wording with your name taken out, I'll tell you which version fits.<|im_end|>

Put down the $2,300. Here's what I can tell you about the back end, and then a faster route that doesn't need your signature on a false number.

I can't see your county's system. A fill-in caseworker on the phone can't promise you how it will treat you either. What I can tell you is how these applications generally work. At the end you certify that what you entered is true, usually under penalty of law. Some programs check bank records or ask for statements. Some check a sample, and some check months later. If yours checks and finds savings you listed as zero, a few things can happen. The mildest is a hold while they sort it out, which is the very delay you're trying to avoid. After that come denial, a demand to pay the money back, and in the worse cases a fraud referral. A referral is less common for amounts like yours, but it's the outcome that stays attached to your name the next time you need help. And "a caseworker told me to" won't protect you much. You signed the form. He didn't.

One more thing, and I'll only say it once. If the fast lane is there for people with nothing at all, every false zero pushes a real zero further back in the line. Lots of people may be doing it, so you wouldn't be the worst of them. It still costs somebody.

Now the 9 days, which is the actual emergency.

1. Call the county ERAP office today with the eviction notice in front of you. Ask: "I have a notice from my landlord's attorney and 9 days before it goes to the sheriff. Is there a priority track for imminent eviction, and what do you need from me to get on it?" Many programs have exactly this. It's the honest way into the fast queue, and it was built for people in your spot.
2. Ask the savings question directly, in writing if you can: "My income is $0. Does listing savings change eligibility or routing, and what does asset verification require?" Then attach your bank statement to the application up front. If the slow part is staff chasing documents, give them the document before they have to ask.
3. Call legal aid or a local tenant hotline today, before you submit. Eviction rules vary a lot by state and county. In some places a pending assistance application can pause enforcement, and in others a judge can grant time. I don't know which rules apply to you. A tenant lawyer will know after one phone call, and a 9-day deadline is exactly the kind of thing they deal with.
4. When you submit, get the confirmation number and email it to the landlord's lawyer with the date and the program name. A lot of landlords would rather wait a few weeks for county money than pay to finish an eviction. Not all of them, but it costs you one email.
5. Write down every call: who you spoke to, when, and what they said.

About the savings: with no income, keeping $2,300 as your only cushion makes sense, and it's your call. The one time I'd think about using some of it is if the landlord's lawyer will hold off in return for a partial payment while the application goes through. A dead car or a medical bill would be bad. Losing the apartment is usually worse, and it costs more to come back from. You know your numbers better than I do.

If you tell me your county, I can help you find the program's priority criteria and the local legal aid number.<|im_end|>

The plan your friend describes is not a good one. It creates practical problems you probably have not considered, and it puts you in the position of telling Dana one thing while preparing to do another. She has been straight with you for six years. You should be straight with her.

Look at what filing that notice actually involves. In most states, a notice to quit or a notice to pay or quit has to be served on the tenant. Dana will see it the day it is served. There is no quiet version. If you have already agreed to take five hundred dollars less, she is not behind on the rent you agreed to accept. A notice saying otherwise contradicts your own deal, and a judge is likely to throw it out. These notices also run for short periods, often just a few days to two weeks, and in many states if you accept rent after serving one, you have waived it and must serve a new one later. So filing now does not bank time for you the way your friend suggests.

There is also what happens to Dana if this ever reaches court. In most places, an eviction filing becomes public record. It can appear on tenant screening reports even if the case is later dismissed. For a tenant who has never been late in six years, that is a serious and lasting harm.

If you want to help her and protect yourself, do it plainly. Put the agreement in writing. One page is enough. State the reduced amount, the exact months it covers, the date full rent resumes, and whether the five hundred dollars a month is forgiven or deferred and to be repaid on a schedule. Add a line that all other lease terms remain the same. Both of you sign it. If she later fails to pay what you agreed, you have a clear and provable default.

Think carefully about what you can actually afford. Since any discount comes straight out of the money that pays your mortgage, you might consider deferring part of the rent rather than reducing it, or taking a smaller cut, or splitting it so that two hundred and fifty dollars is forgiven and two hundred and fifty dollars is deferred. Pick a number you will not resent in the third month.

There are other places to look for help. Dana may be eligible for unemployment benefits, and some local or state governments run emergency rental assistance programs that sometimes pay the landlord directly. It is also worth calling your own mortgage lender to ask if they have any short-term hardship options. That is not guaranteed, but it is one phone call.

Put a date in the written agreement to talk again before the two or three months are up, so you both know where things stand.

If the situation does eventually require eviction, the usual process is this. You serve a pay-or-quit notice that meets your state's rules on how it must be written, delivered, and how much time it must give the tenant, often three to fourteen days. If the rent is still not paid, you file an eviction complaint in the local court, and a hearing is typically set within one to four weeks. If you win, the court issues a judgment and then a writ of possession, which the sheriff or marshal enforces, often within days to a couple of weeks. From start to finish that is roughly a month or two in faster states and several months in slower ones, especially if the tenant contests.

Before you serve anything, check your state's statute or talk to a local landlord-tenant attorney. A technical mistake in the notice sends you back to the beginning, which costs more time than your friend's shortcut could ever save.<|im_end|>
